title: A multi-center clinical trial of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in transfusion-dependent thalassemia

paper_content.abstract: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has recently been approved as standard therapy for transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) but remains limited to the use of HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs), due to a lack of large-scale prospective studies evaluating the use of grafts from alternative donors. Here, we report the results of a non-randomised, interventional, phase 4 clinical trial evaluating allo-HSCT from alternative donors for the treatment of TDT. A total of 823 patients with TDT were transplanted with grafts from MSDs (n=331) or alternative donors, including matched unrelated donors (MUDs; n=352) and haploidentical related donors (Haplos; n=140). Conditioning was with busulfan, cyclophosphamide, fludarabine and anti-thymocyte globulin. Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis was cyclosporine, methotrexate (MTX) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) for recipients of MSDs and tacrolimus, MTX, MMF for others. The primary endpoints were 2-year overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS). Two-year OS for MSDs, MUDs, Haplos was 97.2% (95% CI, 95.4-99.0), 93.1% (90.5-95.9) and 95.4% (91.9-99.1); EFS was 97.2% (95.4-99.0), 92.9% (90.1-95.7) and 94.7% (90.9-98.6); GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 91.4% (88.4-94.6), 77.0% (72.6-82.7) and 75.6% (68.5-83.4) respectively. Two-year OS and EFS for MUDs were lower than those for MSDs (both P<0.05) and were not significantly different with those for Haplos (both P>0.05). Transplant-related mortality was 4.4% (3.0-5.9) and graft failure rate was 0.5%. The incidence of grades 2-4 acute GvHD and moderate-severe chronic GvHD from alternative donors were higher than those from MSDs (28.9% [24.7-33.2] vs 7.5% [4.9-10.7], P<0.001; 12.3% [9.2-15.7] vs 5.0% [2.9-7.9], P<0.01). In summary, these findings may help expand the donor pool for patients with TDT lacking MSDs (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04009525).
paper_content.introduction:
The hemoglobinopathies thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD) are common genetic diseases. Approximately 300,000 SCD infants and 40,000 β-thalassemia infants are born annually and these variants consume huge health-care resources, related to life-long iron chelation and blood transfusions. Over 80% of these patients live in low or middle-income countries, and less than 15% of patients with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) live beyond 35 years due to inadequate treatments. Thus, curative strategies, i.e., allogeneic hemopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) and/or gene therapy are needed.

Allo-HSCT with HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs) has been standard therapy for TDT patients, event-free survival (EFS) reaching 80–90%. Unfortunately, MSDs could be found for only 25–30% of TDT patients. Alternative donors (matched unrelated donors [MUDs] and haploidentical related donors [Haplos]) have been explored, but allo-HSCT with alternative donors is characterized by high rates of graft failure (GF), and graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), yielding inferior overall survival (OS) and EFS compared with MSDs. Although alternative donor outcomes have been comparable with MSDs in hematological malignancies, their use for TDT is still investigational, and a lack of large-scale prospective studies prevents the application of alternative donor allo-HSCT for TDT.

We previously reported a 3-year EFS of 97% after allo-HSCT for 184 TDT patients with MSDs, using the protocol GX-07-TM. With support from the Chinese Red Cross and the Guangxi local government, we launched the project Severe Thalassemia Patients Treatment Plan in 2019, aiming to promote allo-HSCT for TDT and transplant patients within three years. We designed this prospective, multi-center trial to confirm our previous results and to assess outcomes using alternative donors.
paper_content.results:
Patients
Between July 5, 2019, and July 31, 2023, 841 patients from 16 Chinese centers were screened. Eighteen patients met the exit criteria, and 823 patients were eligible for the final analysis, including 787 with β-TDT and 36 with α-TDT. Among them, 331 received transplants from MSDs and 492 from alternative donors, comprising 352 MUDs and 140 Haplos. Median follow-up after transplantation was 23 months (IQR 13–36, range 3–52). The last follow-up was October 31, 2023.

Engraftment and graft failure
The median time to neutrophil engraftment was 12 days (IQR 11–14), 12 days (IQR 11–13) and 12 days (IQR 11–14) in MSDs, MUDs and Haplos, respectively. The median time to platelet engraftment was 14 days (IQR 12–20), 12 days (IQR 11–15) and 14 days (IQR 12–17) in the three type donors. Neutrophil engraftment did not differ between MSDs, MUDs and Haplos. Compared with MSDs and Haplos, the median time to platelet engraftment was less in MUDs (p<0.01). Primary engraftment was achieved in 819 patients, 4 patients experienced GF (GF was 0.5%; 1 primary GF, 3 secondary GF, 2 died and 2 became transfusion dependent).

Primary endpoints
The primary endpoint was achieved. The observed 2-year OS was 95.2%, significantly exceeding the predefined reference value of 91.5% (P<0.001). Two-year OS and EFS were 95.2% (95% confidence interval (CI), 93.7–96.7), and 94.9% (93.4–96.5) for all patients, with both 97.2% (95.4–99.0) for MSDs, 93.1% (90.5–95.9) and 92.9% (90.1–95.7) for MUDs, 95.4% (91.9–99.1) and 94.7% (90.9–98.6) for Haplos. The 2-year GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 82.7% (80.0–85.4) for all patients, 91.4% (88.4–94.6) for MSDs, and 77.0% (72.6–81.7) for MUDs and 75.6% (68.5–83.4) for Haplos. In a post hoc analysis, 800 patients with MUDs and Haplos had slightly lower OS and EFS, and higher transplant-related mortality (TRM) compared with MSDs recipients. There was no center-dependent effect observed for these results.

In univariate analysis, OS and EFS were significantly lower for MUDs compared to MSDs (hazard ratio (HR) 2.74, 95% CI 1.25–5.99; P=0.012 and HR 2.90, 95% CI 1.33–6.32; P=0.007, respectively), for splenectomy group compared to non-splenectomy (3.35, 1.66–6.76; P=0.001 and 3.12, 1.56–6.24; P=0.001), for patients older than 15 years (4.86, 1.91–12.36; P=0.001 and 4.48, 1.79–11.23; P=0.001), and for patients with grades 2–4 and 3–4 acute GvHD (aGvHD) compared to those without aGvHD (5.59, 2.91–10.72; P<0.001 and 5.08, 2.69–9.59; P<0.001 for 2–4 aGvHD, respectively; 10.39, 5.39–20.04; P<0.001 and 9.59, 5.00–118.16; P<0.001 for 3–4 aGvHD, respectively). OS and EFS were significantly lower in patients with infections (13.30, 1.73–101.93; P=0.013 and 7.68, 1.70–34.68; P=0.008, respectively), cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation (2.45, 1.27–4.74; P=0.008 and 2.54, 1.32–4.87; P=0.005, respectively) and hemorrhagic cystitis (HC) (2.46, 1.29–4.69; P=0.006 and 2.85, 1.52–5.35; P=0.001, respectively), compared to unaffected patients. Additionally, EFS was also lower in patients with veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS) (3.62, 1.29–10.18; P=0.015) compared to those without VOD/SOS. The total number of CD34+ cells infused showed a protective effect; thus, OS were improved with higher CD34+ cell doses infused (0.89, 0.82–0.98; P=0.013). Factors that have a negative impact on OS and EFS are found in Supplementary Table 3. Post hoc multivariable analysis of risk factors for OS and EFS showed that grades 2–4 aGvHD (HR 5.24, 95% CI 2.70–10.20 and 4.56, 2.40–8.69), age >15 years (3.07, 1.06–8.88 and 2.88, 1.01–8.23), and previous splenectomy (3.36, 1.49–7.54 and 3.15, 1.41–7.02) were significant negative predictors for OS and EFS compared to patients without these risk factors.

Secondary endpoints
The cumulative incidence of grades 2–4, and 3–4 aGvHD was 7.5% (95% CI, 4.9–10.7) and 1.9% (0.8–3.9) in patients for MSDs, 27.6% (22.8–32.6) and 14.6% (10.8–18.9) for MUDs and 32.3% (24.2–40.6) and 14.7% (8.9–21.9) for Haplos. Two-year cumulative incidence of chronic GvHD (cGvHD) and moderate-severe cGvHD was 8.5% (5.7–12.0) and 5.0% (2.9–7.9) for MSDs, 19.1% (14.8–23.9) and 11.2% (7.9–15.2) for MUDs, and 22.6% (15.2–30.8) and 15.1% (8.9–22.9) for Haplos. Among the 668 patients with follow-up longer than one year, cGvHD occurred in 8.9% (5.9–12.5) of MSDs and 18.8% (14.3–23.8) for MUDs and 23.1% (15.5–31.7) for Haplos; moderate–severe cGvHD occurred in 5.4% (3.2–8.5) for MSDs, 10.7% (7.3–14.8) for MUDs and 14.7% (8.4–22.7) for Haplos, respectively. These analyses show a consistent pattern of higher cGvHD rates after alternative donors (MUDs and Haplos) than after MSDs. Of the 112 cases of cGvHD were recorded, 56% had prior aGvHD. The organ scores of cGvHD were shown in Supplementary Table 5.

In univariable analysis, MUDs (HR 4.09, 95% CI 2.62–6.37; HR 7.00, 95% CI 3.15–15.60) and Haplos (5.03, 3.06–8.27; 7.35, 3.05–17.70) increased risk for grades 2–4 and 3–4 aGvHD compared with MSDs. For moderate-severe cGvHD, the risks were significantly higher for patients with MUDs (2.21, 1.24–3.94) and Haplos (2.58, 1.30–5.10), compared to MSDs. History of aGvHD markedly influenced cGvHD risk (4.42, 2.74–7.14 for grades 2–4 aGvHD; 8.03, 4.74–13.60 for grades 3–4 aGvHD). The proportion of patients with moderate-severe cGvHD at 2 years is shown in Table 2.

Post hoc multivariable analysis revealed that the risk of grades 2–4 and 3–4 aGvHD was significantly higher in patients with MUDs (HR 3.38, 95% CI 1.74–6.58 for grades 2–4; 7.37, 2.12–25.56 for grades 3–4) and Haplos (4.89, 2.88–8.30 for grades 2–4; 7.59, 3.07–18.79 for grades 3–4), compared to MSDs. Additionally, grades 2–4 aGvHD were associated with an increased risk of developing moderate-severe cGvHD (3.80, 2.29–6.32).

Safety
Infectious complications exhibited notable variations among donor types. Haplo-patients had higher incidences of pneumonia (48.6%), CMV (52.1%) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) (32.9%) reactivation compared with those having MSDs and MUDs. Moreover, the rates of bacterial and fungal infections, septicemia, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) were similar between groups. VOD/SOS, diagnosed in 27 patients (3.3%), without difference between the subgroups. Hemorrhagic cystitis was observed in 190 (23.0%) patients, 48 (14.5%) were MSDs, 99 (28.1%) MUDs, and 43 (30.7%) Haplos, respectively, for all SAEs see Supplementary Table 8.

The overall 2-year TRM was 4.4% (95% CI, 3.0–5.9) for all patients, 2.5% (0.8–4.2) for MSDs, 6.3% (3.7–9.9) for MUDs, and 4.6% (0.9–8.1%) for Haplos. The main causes of death in 38 cases were infections (two patients died from the COVID-19 infection), GvHD and intracranial hemorrhage. Fifty-four (6.6%) patients developed mixed chimerism (MC) at a median of 133 (range 15–574) days. The 12.4% MC in patients with MSDs was higher than 3.1% in MUDs and 1.4% in Haplos. There was no significant difference in outcome for patients ages 2–7 and 7–15 years, but patients over 15 years exhibited lower two-year OS, EFS, and higher TRM than the younger cohort(s). After adjustment for age and hepatomegaly (>5cm), the 92 splenectomised patients still had inferior OS, EFS, and increased TRM, although they had faster neutrophil and platelet engraftment compared with non-splenectomised patients. The infection-related mortality in splenectomised group was higher than that in non-splenectomised patients (7.6% vs 2.5%, P=0.010).

Outcomes
Primaryendpoints were 2-year OS and EFS, OS defined as time from transplant to death from any cause, or censored at time of last follow-up. EFS was defined as the time from transplantation to death from any cause, graft failure, or recurrence of transfusion dependence. The FAS included all patients who underwent transplantation and received at least one dose of the conditioning regimen, GF or recurrent TDT, similarly censored for patients alive. Secondary endpoints were aGvHD and cGvHD, neutrophil and platelet recovery, engraftment of donor cells, TRM, GF incidence, incidence of serious infections, reactivations of CMV, adenovirus, EBV, and MC. GRFS at 2 years was defined as free events including grades 3–4 aGvHD, cGvHD requiring systemic treatment, thalassemia relapse, or death from any cause. GvHD was classified by the Glucksberg and NIH classifications. Neutrophil and Platelet engraftment, TRM, GF, MC were defined as in prior studies. The diagnosis of VOD/SOS was according to McDonald. The number of adverse events and organism group (bacteria, virus, or fungus) were provided for infections.

Statisticalanalysis
Two-year OS after allo-HSCT was ~91.5% without distinguishing between donor types according to previous reports. Assuming a 2-year OS of at least 94% to be significantly different from the null targeted value of 91.5% for a two-sided α-level of 5%, power of 90% and a dropout rate of 15%, with recruitment time of 36 months and follow-up time of 12 months, ~800 patients were required.

We summarized data using medians and interquartile ranges, or proportions, and made comparisons with Kruskal–Wallis test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Chi-square test or Fisher Exact test, as appropriate. For the OS, EFS, GRFS, and TRM, time-to-event rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and hazard ratios were estimated using the Cox proportional hazards model with centers as a random-effect. For complications such as MC, VOD/SOS, HC, PRES and infections, the odds ratio was estimated using the Logistic model. In the presence of competing risks, the Fine and Gray model was used for GvHD. The risk factors included in the multivariate analysis were predetermined according to their importance and presumed relevance to outcome. SPSS v23.0 and R v4.2.1 were used for analysis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I commend the authors for a large prospective transplant trial in TDT. There are big numbers and there is no centre effect in
outcomes and these are important. Transplanting patients at a young age is also important
There are many patients, including those receiving MSD, MUD and haplo-identical donors
The TRM is low
It is a well written manuscript. The separation of methods (including references) from the rest of the manuscript was
confusing to me
Major comments
1) The conditioning regimen is Flu Cy ATG and Busufan. This must appear in the abstract and not simply reference the trials
acronym.
a) this is descrobed as intensive conditioning- the authors should clarify that this is intensively immunosuppressive but not
myelosuppresive
b) the authors should clarify if busulfan levels were used and what the target pK was if so
c) the authors should make clear that in the absence of pK the low incidence of VOD etc might simply reflect low exposure to
busulfan
2) There is low graft failure. The authors comment that graft failure is due to the immune suppression and that that intensive
T-cell immune suppression of the recipient facilitates engraftment. Achieving engraftment in transplant is facilitated by
intensive myeloblation, and by the immune action of donor cells. Part of the engraftment is therefore facilitated by aGVHD
(27 and 32% in the MUD and haplo) and chronic GVHD (19 and 22% respectively). Of course patients with GVHD will have
donor cell engraftment.
Late "graft failure" in TDT is usually autologous reconstitution and reflects inadequate myelosuppression rather than
rejection as such, and retransplant can be performed with the same donor, and with success. This further argues that this is
not a T-cell phenomenon, or not simply.
3) The acute and the chronic GVHD rates are high and this must be an important message of the article and must appear in
the abstract. Gvhd free, DFS is the most important endpoint, and in Non malignant diseases like TDT then this must be the
goal of transplant
a) The GVHD prophylaxis for MSD in TDT including T-cell depleting serotherapy is standard and should be stated as such
b) GVHD will be risked by usng PBSC etc in the MUD
c) The GVHD prophylaxis in the haplosetting is far from standard and most institutions would use PTCy or αβ-T cell
depletion to achieve engraftment without GVHD, The authors should address why they used a similar GVHD prophylaxis in
the mismatched setting, and what would be their recommendations going forward
d) what is the quality of life in those with cGVHD. In TDT there is medical alternative therapy and perhaps this might be
preferred and have a higher quality of life than those with cGVHD

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Liu et al provide the results of a prospective multi-center trial of allogeneic stem cell transplantation for thalassemia from
China. The study is distinguished by its large sample size, uniform treatment protocol, and comparison of multiple donor
sources for stem cells. There has been a persistent effort to expand the availability of alternative-donor SCT to patients
lacking matched-sibling donors in countries with high prevalence of thalassemia major, particularly Thailand, India, and
China.
The barriers to the adoption of alternative donors for thalassemia are transplant-related mortality, graft failure, and cGVHD.
With an observed EFS 93-97%, the study team has easily overcome the first two challenges. Among recipients of alternative
donors, cGVHD was observed in approximately 20%, with moderate to severe cGVHD in 11-15% of recipients.
Comments:
1. The difference in EFS between the MSD and MUD/HID groups is small, but there is a notable gap in GVHD and relapse-
free survival (GRFS, 91% vs 77%). To appreciate the significance of this observation, please describe the health status of
patients with cGVHD at the last follow-up.
a. Under ‘Secondary Endpoints’ on cGVHD, please provide information on functional status and immunosuppression.
b. The observed incidence of cGVHD may underestimate the true incidence due to the short post-transplant period for some
patients. Can the authors provide the incidence of cGVHD in patients with follow-up greater than 1 year?
2. The use of post-transplant iron chelation in patients following engraftment is uncommon, as phlebotomy is generally
preferred to treat iron overload. Please add the rationale for recommending chelation therapy.
3. The study protocol uses the same intensive conditioning for MSD and alternative donors. Could some patients in the MSD
group be treated with less immunosuppressive regimens?
4. The impact of splenectomy on post-transplant outcomes is a significant observation. Please discuss whether infection-
associated mortality differed between splenectomized and non-splenectomized groups.
5. Please provide genotypes of patients with alpha thalassemia in Table 1.
a. The anemia in many forms of hemoglobin H disease responds to splenectomy. Was this considered as an option before
transplant, where applicable?
b. The discussion (Line 294, page 11) on splenectomy prior to transplant should distinguish between genotypes. I agree with
avoiding splenectomy in beta thalassemia syndromes. However, splenectomy is an important option for patients with alpha-
thalassemia who require regular transfusions.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Reviewers,
We are grateful for the opportunity to submit the revised version of our manuscript, entitled “A
Multi-center Clinical Trial of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in Transfusion
Dependent Thalassemia”, along with a detailed point-by-point response to the reviewers’ comments.
Following the reviewers’ constructive and insightful feedback, we have undertaken substantial
revisions to strengthen the manuscript. Key improvements include:
1. Clarification and expansion of the conditioning regimen, including explicit description in the
Abstract and a more detailed explanation of the immunosuppressive versus myeloablative
components.
2. Addition of busulfan pharmacokinetic context, incorporating evidence from Chinese HSCT
cohorts and acknowledging the lack of routine therapeutic drug monitoring in most centers.
3. A comprehensive revision of GvHD-related sections, including incidence, prophylaxis
rationale, comparison across donor types, and long-term health status of patients with chronic
GvHD.
4. Enhanced analyses addressing reviewer concerns, such as follow-up duration, chronic GvHD
incidence after one year, rationale for post-transplant iron chelation, impact of splenectomy on
infection-related mortality, and α-thalassemia specific considerations.
5. Clarification of methodology and endpoints, including alignment of definitions for EFS/FAS
and explicit confirmation that the primary endpoint was met.
6. Strengthened discussion of limitations, including non-randomized design, short follow-up for
late effects, and generalizability across ethnic groups.
7. Supplemented the required materials, including reporting summary and source data.
We believe these revisions substantially improve the scientific rigor, clarity, and translational
relevance of the manuscript. Importantly, our prospective multicenter dataset-the largest to date in
transfusion-dependent thalassemia-provides high-quality real-world evidence supporting safe and
effective allogeneic transplantation across donor types, particularly in resource-limited regions.
We thank the reviewers for their careful evaluation and insightful recommendations, which have
significantly improved the quality of our work. We hope that the revised manuscript now meets the
high standards of Nature Communications.
We remain at your disposal for any further information.
Sincerely,
Yongrong Lai, MD, PhD
Department of Hematology,
the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Guangxi, China

b) the authors should clarify if busulfan levels were used and what the target pK was if so
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. Busulfan PK was not routinely monitored due to
multicenter constraints; however, dosing followed body surface area-based guidelines, consistent
with established pediatric protocols. In some thalassemia patients transplants conducted at our
center, Bu was administered intravenously at 1.0 mg/kg per dose, four times daily. PK assessment
consistently showed busulfan plasma concentrations within the range required for effective
myeloablation (target AUC ≈ 900–1,500 µM·min). Second, Bu PK have been evaluated in several
studies involving Chinese patients. A pharmacokinetic analysis conducted at the Blood and Marrow
Transplantation Center of Ruijin Hospital enrolled 45 patients with hematologic malignancies
undergoing allogeneic HSCT. In this study, patients received intravenous Bu at a dose of 1.6
mg/kg. The findings showed that intravenous Bu exposure in Chinese patients was generally lower
than that reported in Caucasian populations, contributing to the Bu plasma concentrations in our
cohort.
Table. Bu PK from some thalassemia patients transplants was conducted at our center.
Revised text (Discussion)
The other limitation is that we did not monitor the intravenous Bu levels for most patients because it
was unavailable at most Chinese HSCT centers, although the Bu pharmacokinetic data in small
number TDT patients showed plasma concentrations within the effective myeloablative range.
Previous studies indicate that intravenous Bu exposure is lower in Chinese than in Caucasian
patients33, suggesting ethnic metabolic differences. Thus, the GX-07-TM protocol may require dose
adjustment for different ethnic populations to ensure optimal exposure and safety. Despite these
limitations, the prospective multi-center design and standardized treatment approach provide
valuable real-world evidence on allo-HSCT outcomes in TDT across multiple donor types.
c) the authors should make clear that in the absence of pK the low incidence of VOD etc might
simply reflect low exposure to busulfan.
Response
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The incidence of VOD/SOS in this study (3.3%)
was substantially lower than in our previous report (10.4%), which may be attributed to the use of
intravenous BU and extensive clinical experience from over 1,300 thalassemia transplants at our
center. Early recognition of VOD, optimized calcineurin inhibitor management, and effective
hepatic protection strategies also contributed to this improvement. These above Bu PK assessments
confirmed exposure within the myeloablative range, while the low VOD incidence indicates that
excessive BU exposure was effectively avoided under the GX-07-TM protocol.
Revised text (Discussion)
The incidence of VOD/SOS in this study (3.3%) was substantially lower than in our previous report
(10.4%), which may be attributed to the use of intravenous Bu31 and our rich experience of
identifing early symoptoms of VOD/SOS, management of adverse drug reaction such as calcineurin
inhibitors , azoles and so on.
Comment 2
There is low graft failure. The authors comment that graft failure is due to the immune suppression
and that that intensive T-cell immune suppression of the recipient facilitates engraftment. Achieving
engraftment in transplant is facilitated by intensive myeloblation, and by the immune action of
donor cells. Part of the engraftment is therefore facilitated by aGVHD (27 and 32% in the MUD and
haplo) and chronic GVHD (19 and 22% respectively). Of course patients with GVHD will have
donor cell engraftment.
Late "graft failure" in TDT is usually autologous reconstitution and reflects inadequate
myelosuppression rather than rejection as such, and retransplant can be performed with the same
donor, and with success. This further argues that this is not a T-cell phenomenon, or not simply.
Response
We appreciate this insightful comment. We agree that engraftment reflects the combined effects of
conditioning intensity, donor immune activity, and host suppression. While our regimen emphasized
immune suppression, it also provided sufficient myeloablation to prevent autologous reconstitution.
The low rate of late graft failure (<1%) supports the adequacy of marrow ablation. We have
clarified that our regimen balances both immunologic and myeloablative mechanisms rather than
relying solely on T-cell suppression.
Revised text (Discussion):
In addition, late graft failure in TDT often reflects autologous reconstitution from insufficient
myeloablation rather than immune rejection. Our regimen’s strong myeloablative component,
together with high CD34+ doses and early chimerism-guided interventions, likely minimized this
risk and contributed to the exceptionally low GF rate.
Comment 3
The acute and the chronic GVHD rates are high and this must be an important message of the article
and must appear in the abstract. Gvhd free, DFS is the most important endpoint, and in Non malignant diseases like TDT then this must be the
goal of transplant.
Response
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important issue. We have revised the abstract to include
the incidence of acute and chronic GVHD and the 2-year GRFS.
Revised text (Abstract)
Two-year OS, EFS and GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) were 97.2%, 97.2% and 91.4%
for MSDs, 93.1%, 92.9% and 77.0% for MUDs, 95.4%, 94.7% and 75.6% for Haplos. Two-year OS
and EFS for MUDs were lower than those for MSDs and were not significantly different with those
for Haplos. The transplant-related mortality was 4.4% and graft failure rate was 0.5%. The
incidence of grades 2-4 acute GvHD and moderate-severe chronic GvHD from alternative donors
were higher than those from MSDs（28.9% vs 7.5%，P<0.001; 12.3% vs 5.0%, P<0.01).
a)The GVHD prophylaxis for MSD in TDT including T-cell depleting serotherapy is standard and
should be stated as such.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We agree that the GvHD prophylaxis used for
MSD transplants in TDT—comprising a calcineurin inhibitor, methotrexate, and mycophenolate
mofetil combined with ATG or other T-cell depletion could replace a more traditional GvHD
prophylaxis regimen for patients with non-malignant disorders from MSDs.
Revised text (Discussion):
In our opinion, the GvHD prophylaxis regimen of CsA, MTX, MMF and ATG or other T-cell
depleting serotherapy could replace a more traditional GvHD prophylaxis regimen for patients with
non-malignant disorders from MSDs.
b) GVHD will be risked by usng PBSC etc in the MUD.
Response:
We appreciate this important comment. We agree that the use of granulocyte colony-stimulating
factor–mobilized PBSCs in MUD transplants is associated with an increased risk of both acute and
cGvHD compared with bone marrow grafts. In China, however, the national donor registry provides
only PBSC products for unrelated donor transplants; therefore, all MUD recipients in this study
received PBSC grafts in accordance with the national policy.
References:
1. Anasetti C, et al. Peripheral-blood stem cells versus bone marrow from unrelated donors. N
Engl J Med. 2012 Oct 18;367(16):1487-96.
2. Eapen M, et al. Peripheral blood grafts from unrelated donors are associated with increased
acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease without improved survival. Biol Blood Marrow
Transplant. 2007 Dec;13(12):1461-8.
c) The GVHD prophylaxis in the haplosetting is far from standard and most institutions would use
PTCy or αβ-T cell depletion to achieve engraftment without GVHD, The authors should address
why they used a similar GVHD prophylaxis in the mismatched setting, and what would be their
recommendations going forward.
Response and Revised text (Discussion)
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Optimizing GvHD prophylaxis regimens for
patients receiving transplants from alternative donors remains essential to further improve outcomes.
Recent studies suggest that PTCy, αβ–T cell depletion, or the addition of CD25 antibody to our
prophylaxis protocols can promote durable engraftment while reducing the risk of GvHD.
d) what is the quality of life in those with cGVHD. In TDT there is medical alternative therapy and
perhaps this might be preferred and have a higher quality of life than those with cGVHD.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important point. Chronic GvHD is a major determinant of
long-term quality of life (QoL) after transplantation, particularly in nonmalignant disorders such as
TDT. In our cohort, most cGvHD cases were mild to moderate. We have added a description of
QoL outcomes in the Discussion section.
Revised text (Discussion):
We previously reported the quality of life for TDT patients after allo-HSCT using the GX-07-TM
protocol. The results shown chronic GvHD was independently associated with lower health-related
quality-of-life scores and patients more than 4 years after transplantation achieved an health-related
quality of life equal to that of their healthy peers32.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Comment 1
I read with interest this paper reporting results from a multicentre study. It is a well written
exhaustive report. Obviously the fact that it is an uncontrolled trial marks the limits and this should
be acknowledged as a limitation in the Discussion paragraph.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. We fully agree that the absence of a
randomized control arm is an important limitation of this multicenter study. Our trial was designed
as a pragmatic, prospective cohort study to evaluate the real-world applicability of the GX-07-TM
regimen across diverse donor types in TDT. While the large sample size and standardized treatment
protocol reduce selection bias, the lack of randomization may limit direct comparisons with other
conditioning regimens or control populations. We have now explicitly acknowledged this limitation
in the Discussion section.
Revised text (Discussion):
Limitations include the non-randomized design, relatively short follow-up, which precludes full
assessment of long-term engraftment, late complications, or secondary malignancies, though
ongoing surveillance continues.
Comment 2
I have no major issues but there are some inconsistencies between the protocol and the paper.
For example events for EFS are defined in a different way and the FAS is defined twice in the
protocol with different definitions. Authors should solve these inconsistencies.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have carefully reviewed the protocol and
manuscript to ensure complete consistency in the definitions of both the EFS endpoint and the FAS.
In the revised version, EFS is consistently defined as the time from transplantation to the first event,
including death from any cause, graft failure, or recurrence of transfusion dependence. The FAS is
now clearly defined as all enrolled patients who underwent transplantation and received at least one
dose of conditioning therapy. These corrections have been harmonized across the Methods and
Resultssections to match the protocol.
Revised text (Methods, Outcomes):
EFS was defined as the time from transplantation to death from any cause, graft failure, or
recurrence of transfusion dependence. The FAS included all patients who underwent transplantation
and received at least one dose of the conditioning regimen.
Comment 3
Moreover sample size was determined to assess a difference between 2-years overall survival rate
and the fixed value of 91.5% but nothing is reported about this statistical testing that will be quite
significant, I guess. Please start the Result paragraph reporting if the primary endpoint was either
met or not.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important observation. The sample size of our study was calculated
based on detecting a 2-year OS rate significantly higher than the reference value of 91.5%, with 80%
power and a one-sided α of 0.025. In the final analysis, the observed 2-year OS was 95.2% (95% CI,
94.0–97.0; P<0.001 vs. 91.5%), confirming that the primary endpoint was met with statistical
significance. We have now included this explicit statement at the beginning of the Results section.
Revised text (Results, Primary endpoints):
The primary endpoint was achieved. The observed 2-year OS was 95.2%, significantly exceeding
the predefined reference value of 91.5% (P<0.001).
Comment 4
In figure 1 the total number of alternative donor is 492.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for noting this point. The number of alternative donor transplants was
correctly 492, comprising 352 MUDs and 140 Haplos transplants. We have clarified this explicitly
in both the Results section and the Figure 1 legend to ensure consistency across the manuscript.
Revised text (Results, Patients):
Eighteen patients met the exit criteria, and 823 patients were eligible for the final analysis, including
787 with β-TDT and 36 with α-TDT. Among them, 331 received transplants from MSDs and 492
from alternative donors, comprising 352 MUDs and 140 Haplos.
Revised figure legend (Figure 1):
Patient distribution by donor type: MSDs (n=331), MUDs (n=352), and Haplos (n=140).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Comment 1
The difference in EFS between the MSD and MUD/HID groups is small, but there is a notable gap
in GVHD and relapse-free survival (GRFS, 91% vs 77%). To appreciate the significance of this
observation, please describe the health status of patients with cGVHD at the last follow-up.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. In our study, the GRFS endpoint included relapse,
death, and clinically significant GvHD. Although the incidence of GvHD remained higher in the
alternative donor group, leading to a lower GRFS compared with MSDs, GvHD-related
complications were effectively managed. Consequently, relapse and mortality rates were low,
resulting in favorable EFS outcomes. Among patients who experienced cGvHD, no relapse was
observed by the last follow-up; two deaths occurred—one due to bronchiolitis obliterans with
pulmonary infection and one due to an accident.
a. Under ‘Secondary Endpoints’ on cGVHD, please provide information on functional status and
immunosuppression.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have now added information on the functional
recovery and immunosuppressive status of patients with cGvHD in Supplementary Table 4. The
organ scores of chronic GvHD showed the information on functional organs status in from 112
patients with cGvHD.
Revised text (Results):
The organ scores of cGvHD were shown in Supplementary Table 4.
b. The observed incidence of cGVHD may underestimate the true incidence due to the short
post-transplant period for some patients. Can the authors provide the incidence of cGVHD in

Comment 2
The use of post-transplant iron chelation in patients following engraftment is uncommon, as
phlebotomy is generally preferred to treat iron overload. Please add the rationale for recommending
chelation therapy.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Although phlebotomy is commonly used for
post-transplant iron reduction, we did not recommend it in our cohort because most donors were
thalassemia carriers and many recipients had early post-transplant hemoglobin levels around 100
g/L, making phlebotomy poorly tolerated and potentially unsafe. Instead, iron chelation was
selected as a safer early strategy. In addition, our team has registered two clinical studies evaluating
deferoxamine and deferasirox after HSCT, which demonstrated that post-transplant chelation is
feasible and well tolerated (data not yet published, ChiCTR2000031229, ChiCTR2000031225).
Comment 3
The study protocol uses the same intensive conditioning for MSD and alternative donors. Could
some patients in the MSD group be treated with less immunosuppressive regimens?
Response:
We agree that immunosuppression can be tailored by donor type. Our conditioning regimen ensured
stable engraftment with a very low incidence of graft failure. Previous studies have shown that graft
failure rates are generally lower in transplants from matched sibling donors compared with
alternative donors. Whether less immunosuppressive regimens could be safely applied to MSDs
recipients remains an important question for future investigation.
Comment 4
The impact of splenectomy on post-transplant outcomes is a significant observation. Please discuss
whether infection-associated mortality differed between splenectomized and non-splenectomized
groups.
Response:
We appreciate this important point. In our cohort, splenectomized patients were generally older and
presented with greater hepatomegaly and higher iron overload before transplantation, which
partially explains their inferior overall and event-free survival. The infection-related mortality in
splenectomized group was higher than that in non-splenectomized patients (7.6% vs 2.5%, P=0.010)
(Supplementary Table 9).
Revised text (Results,Discussion):
The infection-related mortality in splenectomized group was higher than that in non-splenectomized
patients (7.6% vs 2.5%, P=0.010). (Supplementary Table 9).(Results)
Our findings indicate that splenectomy was associated with inferior overall outcomes, although
engraftment of neutrophils and platelets occurred more rapidly in splenectomized patients.
Infection-related mortality was significantly higher in the splenectomized group compared with
non-splenectomized patients. (Discussion)
Comment 5
Please provide genotypes of patients with alpha thalassemia in Table 1.
Response:
There were 36 cases of α-thalassemia in the dataset, which have been categorized according to
different genotypes and incorporated into the description of Table 1.
a. The anemia in many forms of hemoglobin H disease responds to splenectomy. Was this
considered as an option before transplant, where applicable?
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We fully agree that splenectomy
can ameliorate anemia in many forms of HbH disease, particularly in older patients or in those with
pronounced splenomegaly or hypersplenism. This distinction between α- and β-TDT is clinically
meaningful. In our cohort, however, nearly all α-TDT cases were young children with severe
transfusion-dependent phenotypes, for whom splenectomy is generally not recommended. Only two
α-TDT patients had undergone splenectomy before transplantation, and the small number precludes
any definitive conclusions regarding its impact on transplant outcomes. We agree that the role of
splenectomy in α-TDT warrants further study.
b. The discussion (Line 294, page 11) on splenectomy prior to transplant should distinguish between
genotypes. I agree with avoiding splenectomy in beta thalassemia syndromes. However,
splenectomy is an important option for patients with alpha-thalassemia who require regular
transfusions.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and concur with the comment. For patients
presenting with marked splenomegaly before transplantation, splenectomy is recommended prior to
HSCT. If transfusion independence is achieved after splenectomy, HSCT is generally not advised.
RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS’ COMMENTS
We thank the reviewers for their careful evaluation and insightful recommendations.
We hope that the revised manuscript now meets the standards for publication in Nature
Communications.
Sincerely,
Yongrong Lai, MD, PhD
Department of Hematology,
the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Guangxi, China

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has recently been approved as standard therapy for transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) but remains limited to the use of HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs), due to a lack of large-scale prospective studies evaluating the use of grafts from alternative donors. Here, we report the results of a non-randomised, interventional, phase 4 clinical trial evaluating allo-HSCT from alternative donors for the treatment of TDT. A total of 823 patients with TDT were transplanted with grafts from MSDs (n=331) or alternative donors, including matched unrelated donors (MUDs; n=352) and haploidentical related donors (Haplos; n=140). Conditioning was with busulfan, cyclophosphamide, fludarabine and anti-thymocyte globulin. Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis was cyclosporine, methotrexate (MTX) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) for recipients of MSDs and tacrolimus, MTX, MMF for others. The primary endpoints were 2-year overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS). Two-year OS for MSDs, MUDs, Haplos was 97.2% (95% CI, 95.4-99.0), 93.1% (90.5-95.9) and 95.4% (91.9-99.1); EFS was 97.2% (95.4-99.0), 92.9% (90.1-95.7) and 94.7% (90.9-98.6); GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 91.4% (88.4-94.6), 77.0% (72.6-82.7) and 75.6% (68.5-83.4) respectively. Two-year OS and EFS for MUDs were lower than those for MSDs (both P<0.05) and were not significantly different with those for Haplos (both P>0.05). Transplant-related mortality was 4.4% (3.0-5.9) and graft failure rate was 0.5%. The incidence of grades 2-4 acute GvHD and moderate-severe chronic GvHD from alternative donors were higher than those from MSDs (28.9% [24.7-33.2] vs 7.5% [4.9-10.7], P<0.001; 12.3% [9.2-15.7] vs 5.0% [2.9-7.9], P<0.01). In summary, these findings may help expand the donor pool for patients with TDT lacking MSDs (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04009525).

---

## Introduction

The hemoglobinopathies thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD) are common genetic diseases. Approximately 300,000 SCD infants and 40,000 β-thalassemia infants are born annually and these variants consume huge health-care resources, related to life-long iron chelation and blood transfusions. Over 80% of these patients live in low or middle-income countries, and less than 15% of patients with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) live beyond 35 years due to inadequate treatments. Thus, curative strategies, i.e., allogeneic hemopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) and/or gene therapy are needed.

Allo-HSCT with HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs) has been standard therapy for TDT patients, event-free survival (EFS) reaching 80–90%. Unfortunately, MSDs could be found for only 25–30% of TDT patients. Alternative donors (matched unrelated donors [MUDs] and haploidentical related donors [Haplos]) have been explored, but allo-HSCT with alternative donors is characterized by high rates of graft failure (GF), and graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), yielding inferior overall survival (OS) and EFS compared with MSDs. Although alternative donor outcomes have been comparable with MSDs in hematological malignancies, their use for TDT is still investigational, and a lack of large-scale prospective studies prevents the application of alternative donor allo-HSCT for TDT.

We previously reported a 3-year EFS of 97% after allo-HSCT for 184 TDT patients with MSDs, using the protocol GX-07-TM. With support from the Chinese Red Cross and the Guangxi local government, we launched the project Severe Thalassemia Patients Treatment Plan in 2019, aiming to promote allo-HSCT for TDT and transplant patients within three years. We designed this prospective, multi-center trial to confirm our previous results and to assess outcomes using alternative donors.

---

## Results

Patients
Between July 5, 2019, and July 31, 2023, 841 patients from 16 Chinese centers were screened. Eighteen patients met the exit criteria, and 823 patients were eligible for the final analysis, including 787 with β-TDT and 36 with α-TDT. Among them, 331 received transplants from MSDs and 492 from alternative donors, comprising 352 MUDs and 140 Haplos. Median follow-up after transplantation was 23 months (IQR 13–36, range 3–52). The last follow-up was October 31, 2023.

Engraftment and graft failure
The median time to neutrophil engraftment was 12 days (IQR 11–14), 12 days (IQR 11–13) and 12 days (IQR 11–14) in MSDs, MUDs and Haplos, respectively. The median time to platelet engraftment was 14 days (IQR 12–20), 12 days (IQR 11–15) and 14 days (IQR 12–17) in the three type donors. Neutrophil engraftment did not differ between MSDs, MUDs and Haplos. Compared with MSDs and Haplos, the median time to platelet engraftment was less in MUDs (p<0.01). Primary engraftment was achieved in 819 patients, 4 patients experienced GF (GF was 0.5%; 1 primary GF, 3 secondary GF, 2 died and 2 became transfusion dependent).

Primary endpoints
The primary endpoint was achieved. The observed 2-year OS was 95.2%, significantly exceeding the predefined reference value of 91.5% (P<0.001). Two-year OS and EFS were 95.2% (95% confidence interval (CI), 93.7–96.7), and 94.9% (93.4–96.5) for all patients, with both 97.2% (95.4–99.0) for MSDs, 93.1% (90.5–95.9) and 92.9% (90.1–95.7) for MUDs, 95.4% (91.9–99.1) and 94.7% (90.9–98.6) for Haplos. The 2-year GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 82.7% (80.0–85.4) for all patients, 91.4% (88.4–94.6) for MSDs, and 77.0% (72.6–81.7) for MUDs and 75.6% (68.5–83.4) for Haplos. In a post hoc analysis, 800 patients with MUDs and Haplos had slightly lower OS and EFS, and higher transplant-related mortality (TRM) compared with MSDs recipients. There was no center-dependent effect observed for these results.

In univariate analysis, OS and EFS were significantly lower for MUDs compared to MSDs (hazard ratio (HR) 2.74, 95% CI 1.25–5.99; P=0.012 and HR 2.90, 95% CI 1.33–6.32; P=0.007, respectively), for splenectomy group compared to non-splenectomy (3.35, 1.66–6.76; P=0.001 and 3.12, 1.56–6.24; P=0.001), for patients older than 15 years (4.86, 1.91–12.36; P=0.001 and 4.48, 1.79–11.23; P=0.001), and for patients with grades 2–4 and 3–4 acute GvHD (aGvHD) compared to those without aGvHD (5.59, 2.91–10.72; P<0.001 and 5.08, 2.69–9.59; P<0.001 for 2–4 aGvHD, respectively; 10.39, 5.39–20.04; P<0.001 and 9.59, 5.00–118.16; P<0.001 for 3–4 aGvHD, respectively). OS and EFS were significantly lower in patients with infections (13.30, 1.73–101.93; P=0.013 and 7.68, 1.70–34.68; P=0.008, respectively), cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation (2.45, 1.27–4.74; P=0.008 and 2.54, 1.32–4.87; P=0.005, respectively) and hemorrhagic cystitis (HC) (2.46, 1.29–4.69; P=0.006 and 2.85, 1.52–5.35; P=0.001, respectively), compared to unaffected patients. Additionally, EFS was also lower in patients with veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS) (3.62, 1.29–10.18; P=0.015) compared to those without VOD/SOS. The total number of CD34+ cells infused showed a protective effect; thus, OS were improved with higher CD34+ cell doses infused (0.89, 0.82–0.98; P=0.013). Factors that have a negative impact on OS and EFS are found in Supplementary Table 3. Post hoc multivariable analysis of risk factors for OS and EFS showed that grades 2–4 aGvHD (HR 5.24, 95% CI 2.70–10.20 and 4.56, 2.40–8.69), age >15 years (3.07, 1.06–8.88 and 2.88, 1.01–8.23), and previous splenectomy (3.36, 1.49–7.54 and 3.15, 1.41–7.02) were significant negative predictors for OS and EFS compared to patients without these risk factors.

Secondary endpoints

Outcomes
Primaryendpoints were 2-year OS and EFS, OS defined as time from transplant to death from any cause, or censored at time of last follow-up. EFS was defined as the time from transplantation to death from any cause, graft failure, or recurrence of transfusion dependence. The FAS included all patients who underwent transplantation and received at least one dose of the conditioning regimen, GF or recurrent TDT, similarly censored for patients alive. Secondary endpoints were aGvHD and cGvHD, neutrophil and platelet recovery, engraftment of donor cells, TRM, GF incidence, incidence of serious infections, reactivations of CMV, adenovirus, EBV, and MC. GRFS at 2 years was defined as free events including grades 3–4 aGvHD, cGvHD requiring systemic treatment, thalassemia relapse, or death from any cause. GvHD was classified by the Glucksberg and NIH classifications. Neutrophil and Platelet engraftment, TRM, GF, MC were defined as in prior studies. The diagnosis of VOD/SOS was according to McDonald. The number of adverse events and organism group (bacteria, virus, or fungus) were provided for infections.

Statisticalanalysis
Two-year OS after allo-HSCT was ~91.5% without distinguishing between donor types according to previous reports. Assuming a 2-year OS of at least 94% to be significantly different from the null targeted value of 91.5% for a two-sided α-level of 5%, power of 90% and a dropout rate of 15%, with recruitment time of 36 months and follow-up time of 12 months, ~800 patients were required.

We summarized data using medians and interquartile ranges, or proportions, and made comparisons with Kruskal–Wallis test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Chi-square test or Fisher Exact test, as appropriate. For the OS, EFS, GRFS, and TRM, time-to-event rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and hazard ratios were estimated using the Cox proportional hazards model with centers as a random-effect. For complications such as MC, VOD/SOS, HC, PRES and infections, the odds ratio was estimated using the Logistic model. In the presence of competing risks, the Fine and Gray model was used for GvHD. The risk factors included in the multivariate analysis were predetermined according to their importance and presumed relevance to outcome. SPSS v23.0 and R v4.2.1 were used for analysis.

## Paper

## Abstract

Allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has recently been approved as standard therapy for transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) but remains limited to the use of HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs), due to a lack of large-scale prospective studies evaluating the use of grafts from alternative donors. Here, we report the results of a non-randomised, interventional, phase 4 clinical trial evaluating allo-HSCT from alternative donors for the treatment of TDT. A total of 823 patients with TDT were transplanted with grafts from MSDs (n=331) or alternative donors, including matched unrelated donors (MUDs; n=352) and haploidentical related donors (Haplos; n=140). Conditioning was with busulfan, cyclophosphamide, fludarabine and anti-thymocyte globulin. Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis was cyclosporine, methotrexate (MTX) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) for recipients of MSDs and tacrolimus, MTX, MMF for others. The primary endpoints were 2-year overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS). Two-year OS for MSDs, MUDs, Haplos was 97.2% (95% CI, 95.4-99.0), 93.1% (90.5-95.9) and 95.4% (91.9-99.1); EFS was 97.2% (95.4-99.0), 92.9% (90.1-95.7) and 94.7% (90.9-98.6); GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 91.4% (88.4-94.6), 77.0% (72.6-82.7) and 75.6% (68.5-83.4) respectively. Two-year OS and EFS for MUDs were lower than those for MSDs (both P<0.05) and were not significantly different with those for Haplos (both P>0.05). Transplant-related mortality was 4.4% (3.0-5.9) and graft failure rate was 0.5%. The incidence of grades 2-4 acute GvHD and moderate-severe chronic GvHD from alternative donors were higher than those from MSDs (28.9% [24.7-33.2] vs 7.5% [4.9-10.7], P<0.001; 12.3% [9.2-15.7] vs 5.0% [2.9-7.9], P<0.01). In summary, these findings may help expand the donor pool for patients with TDT lacking MSDs (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04009525).

---

## Introduction

The hemoglobinopathies thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD) are common genetic diseases. Approximately 300,000 SCD infants and 40,000 β-thalassemia infants are born annually and these variants consume huge health-care resources, related to life-long iron chelation and blood transfusions. Over 80% of these patients live in low or middle-income countries, and less than 15% of patients with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) live beyond 35 years due to inadequate treatments. Thus, curative strategies, i.e., allogeneic hemopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) and/or gene therapy are needed.

Allo-HSCT with HLA-matched sibling donors (MSDs) has been standard therapy for TDT patients, event-free survival (EFS) reaching 80–90%. Unfortunately, MSDs could be found for only 25–30% of TDT patients. Alternative donors (matched unrelated donors [MUDs] and haploidentical related donors [Haplos]) have been explored, but allo-HSCT with alternative donors is characterized by high rates of graft failure (GF), and graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), yielding inferior overall survival (OS) and EFS compared with MSDs. Although alternative donor outcomes have been comparable with MSDs in hematological malignancies, their use for TDT is still investigational, and a lack of large-scale prospective studies prevents the application of alternative donor allo-HSCT for TDT.

We previously reported a 3-year EFS of 97% after allo-HSCT for 184 TDT patients with MSDs, using the protocol GX-07-TM. With support from the Chinese Red Cross and the Guangxi local government, we launched the project Severe Thalassemia Patients Treatment Plan in 2019, aiming to promote allo-HSCT for TDT and transplant patients within three years. We designed this prospective, multi-center trial to confirm our previous results and to assess outcomes using alternative donors.

---

## Results

Patients
Between July 5, 2019, and July 31, 2023, 841 patients from 16 Chinese centers were screened. Eighteen patients met the exit criteria, and 823 patients were eligible for the final analysis, including 787 with β-TDT and 36 with α-TDT. Among them, 331 received transplants from MSDs and 492 from alternative donors, comprising 352 MUDs and 140 Haplos. Median follow-up after transplantation was 23 months (IQR 13–36, range 3–52). The last follow-up was October 31, 2023.

Engraftment and graft failure
The median time to neutrophil engraftment was 12 days (IQR 11–14), 12 days (IQR 11–13) and 12 days (IQR 11–14) in MSDs, MUDs and Haplos, respectively. The median time to platelet engraftment was 14 days (IQR 12–20), 12 days (IQR 11–15) and 14 days (IQR 12–17) in the three type donors. Neutrophil engraftment did not differ between MSDs, MUDs and Haplos. Compared with MSDs and Haplos, the median time to platelet engraftment was less in MUDs (p<0.01). Primary engraftment was achieved in 819 patients, 4 patients experienced GF (GF was 0.5%; 1 primary GF, 3 secondary GF, 2 died and 2 became transfusion dependent).

Primary endpoints
The primary endpoint was achieved. The observed 2-year OS was 95.2%, significantly exceeding the predefined reference value of 91.5% (P<0.001). Two-year OS and EFS were 95.2% (95% confidence interval (CI), 93.7–96.7), and 94.9% (93.4–96.5) for all patients, with both 97.2% (95.4–99.0) for MSDs, 93.1% (90.5–95.9) and 92.9% (90.1–95.7) for MUDs, 95.4% (91.9–99.1) and 94.7% (90.9–98.6) for Haplos. The 2-year GvHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) was 82.7% (80.0–85.4) for all patients, 91.4% (88.4–94.6) for MSDs, and 77.0% (72.6–81.7) for MUDs and 75.6% (68.5–83.4) for Haplos. In a post hoc analysis, 800 patients with MUDs and Haplos had slightly lower OS and EFS, and higher transplant-related mortality (TRM) compared with MSDs recipients. There was no center-dependent effect observed for these results.

In univariate analysis, OS and EFS were significantly lower for MUDs compared to MSDs (hazard ratio (HR) 2.74, 95% CI 1.25–5.99; P=0.012 and HR 2.90, 95% CI 1.33–6.32; P=0.007, respectively), for splenectomy group compared to non-splenectomy (3.35, 1.66–6.76; P=0.001 and 3.12, 1.56–6.24; P=0.001), for patients older than 15 years (4.86, 1.91–12.36; P=0.001 and 4.48, 1.79–11.23; P=0.001), and for patients with grades 2–4 and 3–4 acute GvHD (aGvHD) compared to those without aGvHD (5.59, 2.91–10.72; P<0.001 and 5.08, 2.69–9.59; P<0.001 for 2–4 aGvHD, respectively; 10.39, 5.39–20.04; P<0.001 and 9.59, 5.00–118.16; P<0.001 for 3–4 aGvHD, respectively). OS and EFS were significantly lower in patients with infections (13.30, 1.73–101.93; P=0.013 and 7.68, 1.70–34.68; P=0.008, respectively), cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation (2.45, 1.27–4.74; P=0.008 and 2.54, 1.32–4.87; P=0.005, respectively) and hemorrhagic cystitis (HC) (2.46, 1.29–4.69; P=0.006 and 2.85, 1.52–5.35; P=0.001, respectively), compared to unaffected patients. Additionally, EFS was also lower in patients with veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS) (3.62, 1.29–10.18; P=0.015) compared to those without VOD/SOS. The total number of CD34+ cells infused showed a protective effect; thus, OS were improved with higher CD34+ cell doses infused (0.89, 0.82–0.98; P=0.013). Factors that have a negative impact on OS and EFS are found in Supplementary Table 3. Post hoc multivariable analysis of risk factors for OS and EFS showed that grades 2–4 aGvHD (HR 5.24, 95% CI 2.70–10.20 and 4.56, 2.40–8.69), age >15 years (3.07, 1.06–8.88 and 2.88, 1.01–8.23), and previous splenectomy (3.36, 1.49–7.54 and 3.15, 1.41–7.02) were significant negative predictors for OS and EFS compared to patients without these risk factors.

Secondary endpoints
The cumulative incidence of grades 2–4, and 3–4 aGvHD was 7.5% (95% CI, 4.9–10.7) and 1.9% (0.8–3.9) in patients for MSDs, 27.6% (22.8–32.6) and 14.6% (10.8–18.9) for MUDs and 32.3% (24.2–40.6) and 14.7% (8.9–21.9) for Haplos. Two-year cumulative incidence of chronic GvHD (cGvHD) and moderate-severe cGvHD was 8.5% (5.7–12.0) and 5.0% (2.9–7.9) for MSDs, 19.1% (14.8–23.9) and 11.2% (7.9–15.2) for MUDs, and 22.6% (15.2–30.8) and 15.1% (8.9–22.9) for Haplos. Among the 668 patients with follow-up longer than one year, cGvHD occurred in 8.9% (5.9–12.5) of MSDs and 18.8% (14.3–23.8) for MUDs and 23.1% (15.5–31.7) for Haplos; moderate–severe cGvHD occurred in 5.4% (3.2–8.5) for MSDs, 10.7% (7.3–14.8) for MUDs and 14.7% (8.4–22.7) for Haplos, respectively. These analyses show a consistent pattern of higher cGvHD rates after alternative donors (MUDs and Haplos) than after MSDs. Of the 112 cases of cGvHD were recorded, 56% had prior aGvHD. The organ scores of cGvHD were shown in Supplementary Table 5.

In univariable analysis, MUDs (HR 4.09, 95% CI 2.62–6.37; HR 7.00, 95% CI 3.15–15.60) and Haplos (5.03, 3.06–8.27; 7.35, 3.05–17.70) increased risk for grades 2–4 and 3–4 aGvHD compared with MSDs. For moderate-severe cGvHD, the risks were significantly higher for patients with MUDs (2.21, 1.24–3.94) and Haplos (2.58, 1.30–5.10), compared to MSDs. History of aGvHD markedly influenced cGvHD risk (4.42, 2.74–7.14 for grades 2–4 aGvHD; 8.03, 4.74–13.60 for grades 3–4 aGvHD). The proportion of patients with moderate-severe cGvHD at 2 years is shown in Table 2.

Post hoc multivariable analysis revealed that the risk of grades 2–4 and 3–4 aGvHD was significantly higher in patients with MUDs (HR 3.38, 95% CI 1.74–6.58 for grades 2–4; 7.37, 2.12–25.56 for grades 3–4) and Haplos (4.89, 2.88–8.30 for grades 2–4; 7.59, 3.07–18.79 for grades 3–4), compared to MSDs. Additionally, grades 2–4 aGvHD were associated with an increased risk of developing moderate-severe cGvHD (3.80, 2.29–6.32).

Safety
Infectious complications exhibited notable variations among donor types. Haplo-patients had higher incidences of pneumonia (48.6%), CMV (52.1%) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) (32.9%) reactivation compared with those having MSDs and MUDs. Moreover, the rates of bacterial and fungal infections, septicemia, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) were similar between groups. VOD/SOS, diagnosed in 27 patients (3.3%), without difference between the subgroups. Hemorrhagic cystitis was observed in 190 (23.0%) patients, 48 (14.5%) were MSDs, 99 (28.1%) MUDs, and 43 (30.7%) Haplos, respectively, for all SAEs see Supplementary Table 8.

The overall 2-year TRM was 4.4% (95% CI, 3.0–5.9) for all patients, 2.5% (0.8–4.2) for MSDs, 6.3% (3.7–9.9) for MUDs, and 4.6% (0.9–8.1%) for Haplos. The main causes of death in 38 cases were infections (two patients died from the COVID-19 infection), GvHD and intracranial hemorrhage. Fifty-four (6.6%) patients developed mixed chimerism (MC) at a median of 133 (range 15–574) days. The 12.4% MC in patients with MSDs was higher than 3.1% in MUDs and 1.4% in Haplos. There was no significant difference in outcome for patients ages 2–7 and 7–15 years, but patients over 15 years exhibited lower two-year OS, EFS, and higher TRM than the younger cohort(s). After adjustment for age and hepatomegaly (>5cm), the 92 splenectomised patients still had inferior OS, EFS, and increased TRM, although they had faster neutrophil and platelet engraftment compared with non-splenectomised patients. The infection-related mortality in splenectomised group was higher than that in non-splenectomised patients (7.6% vs 2.5%, P=0.010).

Comment 2

Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Although phlebotomy is commonly used for
post-transplant iron reduction, we did not recommend it in our cohort because most donors were
thalassemia carriers and many recipients had early post-transplant hemoglobin levels around 100
g/L, making phlebotomy poorly tolerated and potentially unsafe. Instead, iron chelation was
selected as a safer early strategy. In addition, our team has registered two clinical studies evaluating
deferoxamine and deferasirox after HSCT, which demonstrated that post-transplant chelation is
feasible and well tolerated (data not yet published, ChiCTR2000031229, ChiCTR2000031225).

We agree that immunosuppression can be tailored by donor type. Our conditioning regimen ensured

failure rates are generally lower in transplants from matched sibling donors compared with
alternative donors. Whether less immunosuppressive regimens could be safely applied to MSDs
recipients remains an important question for future investigation.

We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and concur with the comment. For patients
presenting with marked splenomegaly before transplantation, splenectomy is recommended prior to
